title: Poor maternal nutrition programmes a pro-atherosclerotic phenotype in ApoE-/- mice.
ehr_evidence: The study used an experimental animal model; pregnant ApoE−/− mice of the C57BL6/J background were fed a control (20% protein) or isocaloric low-protein (8% protein) diet during pregnancy and lactation, with male offspring analysed at 6 months of age.
summary: In a controlled experimental study of ApoE−/− mice, in utero and postnatal exposure to a low-protein diet accelerated atherosclerotic lesion development and progression in 6-month-old male offspring compared with controls.
key_findings: LP offspring had a significantly greater total aortic root plaque area than controls (P < 0.05).
LP offspring had a significantly greater total cholesterol cleft-containing area than controls (P < 0.05).
LP offspring showed a significant reduction in vascular smooth muscle cell content indicated by attenuated SMA positive staining (P < 0.05).
DNA damage marker p-H2AX was significantly increased in atherosclerotic plaque of LP offspring (P < 0.05), whereas inflammatory marker Mac3 and p-ATM were not different between groups.
Total cholesterol (LP 9.77 ± 0.78 vs control 6.73 ± 1.01 mmol/l, P < 0.05) and LDL-cholesterol (LP 8.65 ± 0.70 vs control 4.62 ± 0.70 mmol/l, P < 0.01) were significantly higher in LP offspring.
LP offspring showed a non-significant trend toward elevated insulin, with no significant differences in other lipid measurements or fasting glucose.
Hepatic HMG-CoA reductase expression was significantly increased in LP offspring (P < 0.05), and LDL receptor was elevated (LP 177 ± 38 vs control 100 ± 33).
captured_features: p-ATM cells per 100,000 μm2 plaque area
p-H2AX cells per 100,000 μm2 plaque area
study_design: Experimental controlled diet intervention in an animal model
population: ApoE−/− mice on C57BL6/J background; male offspring analysed at 6 months of age
exposure_domain: Maternal low-protein diet / maternal under-nutrition (fetal programming)
limitations: Findings are limited to a single genetically modified mouse model (ApoE−/−) and may not translate to humans.
Study used only male offspring, limiting generalisability to females.
Small sample sizes (e.g., n = 4–12 per group).
No postnatal atherogenic diet challenge, so lesion development was spontaneous rather than experimentally accelerated.
